1.title: the smallest prayer
1.hook: forehead, chest, shoulder, shoulder: what the hand is tracing
1.carry: head, heart, shoulders — all of you
1.howItsDone: Catholics make the sign of the cross at the start and end of prayers and of the Mass, often after dipping their fingers in holy water on entering a church, touching forehead, chest, left shoulder and right shoulder.

screen: `DAY ONE.`

segments.voice: A pitcher does it before the first throw. A grandmother does it when the bus passes a church. Someone does it in a hospital hallway, right after the doctor leaves. Forehead, chest, one shoulder, the other. Two seconds, no words out loud. If you grew up Catholic, your hand may know it better than your head does. It's a prayer, maybe the smallest there is, and the hand is tracing something on purpose.
screen: `A PITCHER. A GRANDMOTHER. A HOSPITAL HALLWAY.` → `TWO SECONDS.` → `THE SMALLEST PRAYER.`

segments.voice: It's old. Around the year 200, a Christian writer in North Africa described believers tracing a tiny cross on their foreheads all day long: getting dressed, sitting down to eat, lighting a lamp. Over the centuries that thumb-sized cross grew into the big one. And it says two things at once. The hand traces the cross, the shape Jesus died on, over your own body. The words name who Catholics believe God is. They come from the end of Matthew's Gospel, where Jesus sends his friends out, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost." One God: Father, Son and Holy Spirit. That's why many Catholics dip their fingers in holy water at the church door first. Those same words were said over them, with water, at their baptism. Now look where the hand goes. The forehead, where you think. The chest, where your heart is. The shoulders, where you carry things. Many hear it that way: nothing left out. Western Catholics go to the left shoulder first; Orthodox Christians go right, then left. Same sign, two old habits.
screen: `A THUMB ON THE FOREHEAD, AROUND 200.` · `THE CROSS, AND THE NAME.` · `HOLY WATER: A REMINDER OF BAPTISM.` · `THINK, FEEL, CARRY.`

The sign of the cross. The cross traced over all of you, in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. First word on your strand.

2.title: the claim behind the bread
2.hook: a white dress, a party, a wafer: and the claim the day was about
2.tomorrow: the most misunderstood room in the building
2.howItsDone: Catholics receive the Eucharist at Mass, genuflect toward the tabernacle when entering a church, and many spend quiet time in prayer before it, a practice called adoration.

screen: `DAY TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the sign of the cross, all of you in two seconds. Today, the thing at the center of every Mass.
screen: `THE SIGN OF THE CROSS ✓` → `DAY 2.`

segments.voice: A white dress or a clip-on tie. Photos on the church steps, a cake after. First Communion is easy to remember. What the day was actually about can be fuzzier: in surveys, a lot of Catholics describe the bread as a symbol. If it was never spelled out for you, you're not behind: First Communion usually comes at about seven, and that's a lot to hold at seven. The Church's own claim is much bigger than a symbol. So here it is, once, plainly.
screen: `A WHITE DRESS. A CAKE.` → `A SYMBOL?` → `THE CLAIM, ONCE, PLAINLY.`

segments.voice: It starts the night before Jesus died, at a Passover meal. He takes bread, gives thanks, breaks it and says, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "This is my body, which is given for you. Do this for a commemoration of me." Gave thanks, in Greek, is where the word comes from: eucharistia, thanksgiving. Now the claim. Catholics believe that when the priest says those words at Mass, the bread and wine truly become the body and blood of Christ. They still look, taste and feel like bread and wine. What they are, underneath, has changed. Not a symbol of him: him. The Church calls it the real presence. In John's Gospel, Jesus calls himself the living bread, and many followers find that too hard and walk away. He lets them go. After Mass, the consecrated bread that's left is kept in a small box near the altar, the tabernacle, with a red lamp burning beside it. That's why people bend a knee when they walk into an empty church. They believe he's there. Christians differ here. Orthodox Christians and Lutherans also speak of a real presence; many other Protestants see the meal as a memorial and a sign.
screen: `THIS IS MY BODY.` · `EUCHARISTIA — THANKSGIVING.` · `STILL LOOKS LIKE BREAD.` · `THE TABERNACLE AND THE LAMP.`

segments.voice: One breath with the bell. Think of a time someone simply stayed with you: in a waiting room, on the end of your bed, on the phone. They didn't fix anything. Breathe in, remembering it. Breathe out slowly.
The Eucharist. Thanksgiving: the bread and wine Catholics believe become Christ himself, his real presence. Second word.

3.title: the most misunderstood room in the building
3.hook: the booth, the nerves, and why a person and not just a prayer
3.carry: say it out loud, then it's smaller
3.howItsDone: Catholics go to confession with a priest, anonymously behind a screen or face to face, name their sins, receive a small penance, and hear the words of absolution; many go before Christmas and Easter, and some go monthly.

screen: `DAY THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Eucharist, and the claim behind the bread. Today, the room people are most nervous to walk into.
screen: `THE EUCHARIST ✓` → `DAY 3.`

segments.voice: Bless me, Father, for I have sinned. Plenty of people raised Catholic can still say the opening line, and still remember the nerves: the line outside the booth, the list rehearsed in your head, the little screen. Movies made it a courtroom, or a punch line. And later comes the fair question: why tell a person? Why not just tell God?
screen: `BLESS ME, FATHER.` → `THE BOOTH. THE NERVES.` → `WHY A PERSON?`

segments.voice: Catholics call it the sacrament of reconciliation; most just say confession. The answer to why a person starts on Easter night. In John's Gospel, the risen Jesus breathes on his friends and says, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "Whose sins you shall forgive, they are forgiven them." Catholics believe that from then on, forgiveness was meant to be spoken out loud, through a person, and heard out loud too. God does the forgiving; the priest speaks for him, and for the Church, since a wrong never touches just one person. What happens is simple. You can kneel behind a screen or sit face to face. You say what you've done, plainly, in your own words. The priest listens, gives a penance, usually a prayer or a small act to make things right, and then says the words of absolution: you're forgiven, in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. One rule is absolute: the seal. A priest may never reveal what he hears, to anyone, for any reason. And if it's been years, and that's the very thing keeping you away, here's what's true. Mass is open to you; you can go and simply not receive communion until you're ready. You can start with: it's been a long time, and I don't remember how. Priests hear it often, and helping you through is part of the job. Nervous is normal. Some people write their list on a scrap of paper, bring it in, and tear it up afterward. Catholics believe the forgiveness is real even if you walk out feeling awkward, or nothing at all. Something huge in the dark at two in the morning gets edges once it's spoken.
screen: `WHOSE SINS YOU SHALL FORGIVE.` · `BEHIND A SCREEN OR FACE TO FACE.` · `THE SEAL: NEVER REVEALED.` · `SPOKEN, IT HAS EDGES.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. On the first, think of one thing you've been carrying and never said out loud. On the second, name it to yourself in one plain sentence. On the third, breathe out, and notice whether it feels any different now that it has a name.
Confession. Saying it out loud, and hearing out loud that you're forgiven. Third word.

4.title: what the string is for
4.hook: beads on a rearview mirror: counting, not magic
4.howItsDone: Catholics pray the rosary alone or together, some every day, saying an Our Father, ten Hail Marys and a Glory Be for each decade while thinking about a scene from the life of Jesus and Mary.

screen: `DAY FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: confession, the thing said out loud. Today, something that might be hanging from a rearview mirror near you.
screen: `CONFESSION ✓` → `DAY 4.`

segments.voice: A loop of beads swinging from a rearview mirror. Tangled in a grandmother's purse with the car keys and the cough drops. Laid in someone's hands at a funeral. Some people wear one like a necklace; some call it a lucky charm. People can't even agree how many beads are on it. The string is for something much plainer than luck. It's for counting.
screen: `ON A MIRROR. IN A PURSE.` → `A LUCKY CHARM?` → `IT'S FOR COUNTING.`

segments.voice: Rosary comes from the Latin rosarium, a rose garden: a garland of prayers, like a crown of roses. Here's the layout. A cross, a short tail of beads, then the loop: five sets of ten small beads, called decades, each set apart by a single bead. On the single bead, the Our Father. On each of the ten, a Hail Mary. After each ten, a short line of praise, the Glory Be. One decade on its own takes about five minutes, and plenty of people start there. That's where the arguments about the count come from: fifty-nine beads on the whole string, fifty-three Hail Marys. Counting prayers is ancient. Stories from the early desert monks tell of one who kept track of his daily prayers with pebbles in his lap. Later, monks prayed all one hundred and fifty psalms, and tradition says people who couldn't read prayed one hundred and fifty short prayers instead. The rosary grew out of that, and was called the poor man's psalter. And here's the plain secret. While the fingers and lips are busy with the words, the mind is free to think through scenes from the lives of Jesus and Mary, called the mysteries. That's the real prayer. The beads just keep the hands busy.
screen: `ROSARIUM — A ROSE GARDEN.` · `FIVE DECADES OF TEN.` · `PEBBLES IN A MONK'S LAP.` · `THE MIND ON THE MYSTERIES.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. Rest one hand in your lap. On each breath out, touch your thumb to the next finger: one, two, three. Don't count out loud. Let the fingers keep track, so the mind doesn't have to.
The rosary. A garland of prayers on a string that keeps count, so the mind can rest on the life of Jesus. Fourth word.

5.title: honor, not worship
5.hook: "isn't praying to Mary idolatry?" — the answer is one difference
5.howItsDone: Catholics honor Mary and the saints, ask for their prayers, and keep their feast days through the year and on All Saints' Day, November 1; worship is given to God alone.

screen: `DAY FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the rosary, a string that keeps count. Today, the question a friend may have asked you about Mary.
screen: `THE ROSARY ✓` → `DAY 5.`

segments.voice: Sooner or later a friend asks it, usually kindly: why do Catholics pray to Mary? Isn't that worshiping a statue? Walk into an old church and you can see why they'd wonder. Plaster figures in niches. Faces in stained glass. Candles flickering in front of a woman in blue and a man holding keys. Plenty of people raised Catholic were never given the answer either. It turns on one difference, and it's a difference people already live by.
screen: `WHY PRAY TO MARY?` → `A WOMAN IN BLUE. A MAN WITH KEYS.` → `ONE DIFFERENCE.`

segments.voice: Catholics draw a sharp line between worship and honor. Worship belongs to God alone. Honor can be given to people: the way you'd honor a grandmother, a teacher, a hero. Saints get honor. Mary, the mother of Jesus, gets the highest honor of any saint, but still honor, not worship. So why pray to them? Because what Catholics are doing is asking: pray for me. It's what you'd ask a friend. Catholics believe in what the old creed calls the communion of saints: everyone who belongs to Christ, living and dead, is one family, and the family can still pray for each other. Death doesn't end the friendship. So a statue works like a family photo. Nobody is praying to the plaster. And the saints were never perfect. The man with the keys is Peter, who said three times, the night Jesus was arrested, that he didn't know him, then went out and wept. Catholics count him the first pope. A saint isn't someone who never fell. It's someone who kept getting up. Other Christians see it differently: many Protestants honor the saints as examples, and don't ask for their prayers.
screen: `WORSHIP: GOD ALONE.` · `HONOR: MARY AND THE SAINTS.` · `PRAY FOR ME.` · `THE COMMUNION OF SAINTS.`

6.title: ashes, and forty days
6.hook: a smudge on the forehead, fish on Friday: giving something up is a way of paying attention
6.howItsDone: Catholics receive ashes on Ash Wednesday, fast on Ash Wednesday and Good Friday, abstain from meat on Fridays in Lent, and take on prayer, fasting and almsgiving for the forty days before Easter.

screen: `DAY SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the saints, honored, not worshiped. Today, the one day a year Catholics walk around with a smudge on their foreheads.
screen: `THE SAINTS ✓` → `DAY 6.`

segments.voice: One Wednesday a year, a coworker shows up with a black smudge on her forehead. Then the barista. Then a kid on the train. Somebody leans over to say: you've got something on your face. It's Ash Wednesday, and it starts a season. For the next forty days, a Catholic friend might be off chocolate, or off social media, or eating fish on Fridays. It can look like a diet. It isn't about the chocolate.
screen: `A SMUDGE ON THE FOREHEAD.` → `IT'S ASH WEDNESDAY.` → `IT ISN'T ABOUT THE CHOCOLATE.`

segments.voice: Lent is the season of forty days before Easter. Forty is the number the Bible keeps reaching for when someone is being tested: Noah's rain, Moses on the mountain, and Jesus fasting in the desert for forty days before he begins his work. Lent walks alongside those forty days. It opens with ash. A cross is traced on the forehead, often with words from the Bible's first pages, in the Douay-Rheims: "dust thou art, and into dust thou shalt return." It sounds grim. Catholics hear it as honest: you won't be here forever, so what will you do with the time? Then come three old practices: prayer, fasting, and giving to the poor. Catholics fast on Ash Wednesday and Good Friday, and skip meat on the Fridays of Lent, because Friday is the day Jesus died. The rule doesn't count fish as meat. Hello, Friday fish fry. Many also give something up. Here's the idea underneath: give up something small, and every reach for it becomes a moment of noticing. The empty space where the chocolate was becomes a little room for prayer, or for someone else. And the forty days only make sense because of where they end: Easter morning.

7.title: the things your family kept
7.hook: a medal on a keychain, a palm behind the crucifix, an abuela's altarcito: the Church's one word for all of it
7.howItsDone: Catholics use sacramentals such as holy water, blessed medals, rosaries, palms and ashes, ask a priest to bless homes and objects, and keep the devotions of their own families and cultures, from home altars to Simbang Gabi and patron-saint feasts.

screen: `DAY SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Lent, less on purpose. Six words so far: the sign of the cross, the Eucharist, confession, the rosary, the saints, Lent. Today, the seventh.
screen: `THE SIGN OF THE CROSS · THE EUCHARIST · CONFESSION · THE ROSARY · THE SAINTS · LENT`

segments.voice: A Saint Christopher medal on a keychain. A palm from Palm Sunday tucked behind the crucifix, drying out for a year. A bottle of holy water in the kitchen cabinet. An abuela's altarcito, with candles, a rosary and photos of the people she's lost. A Santo Niño, the child Jesus, watching over a Filipino living room. A medal blessed at a quinceañera Mass. Every family's version looks different. The Church has one word for all of it.
screen: `A MEDAL. A PALM. HOLY WATER.` → `AN ALTARCITO. A SANTO NIÑO.` → `ONE WORD FOR ALL OF IT.`

segments.voice: Sacramentals. The word is a cousin of sacrament. The seven sacraments, like baptism, confession and the Eucharist, are the big moments Catholics believe Christ himself gave the Church. Sacramentals are the smaller things the Church added around them: blessings, blessed objects, words and gestures. Look back at this week and you'll find you've been holding them all along. Holy water and the sign of the cross. The ashes. The rosary. A saint's medal. The Church is careful about what they are. They aren't magic, and they aren't lucky charms. They're reminders that help a person get ready for grace, the way a photo on the fridge reminds you to call. Around them grows what the Church calls popular piety: the customs each people builds, which it welcomes as long as they lead back to Christ. So a Filipino family getting up before dawn for nine Masses before Christmas, called Simbang Gabi. A Mexican family's altar for its dead in early November. An Irish grandmother who won't eat meat on any Friday of the year. An Italian town's feast for its patron saint. Different shapes, one faith. Whatever your family's version was, it was a way in.
screen: `SACRAMENTS: THE BIG SEVEN.` · `SACRAMENTALS: THE SMALL SIGNS.` · `NOT MAGIC: REMINDERS.` · `DIFFERENT SHAPES, ONE FAITH.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. Bring to mind one object from your family's faith: a medal, a picture, a candle, a rosary in a drawer. On the first breath, see it. On the second, see whose it was. On the third, let it remind you of them.
Sacramentals. Small blessed things and gestures: reminders that point to grace. Seventh word: a week's worth.

segments.voice: Your line: faith you can hold. That's week one: seven words, and you were already holding most of them. Tomorrow, your grandmother before dinner.

story.title: roses in December
story.text: On a cold December morning in 1531, an Indigenous man named Juan Diego is hurrying past a hill outside what is now Mexico City. A lady stops him there and asks him to tell the bishop to build her a church. The bishop wants proof. So she sends Juan Diego up the bare hilltop, where he finds roses blooming out of season, and he carries them down in his cloak. When he opens it in front of the bishop, the roses spill out, and on the cloth is her image. Mexican Catholics call her Our Lady of Guadalupe, and her picture stands on many family altars.
